Reference: Sant'Anna and Zhao (2020)

Model Setting

The paper studies difference-in-differences (DID) designs with two periods and two groups in which the parallel trends assumption holds only after conditioning on pre-treatment covariates, and asks how to estimate the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT) robustly and efficiently. Two flexible approaches existed: the outcome regression (OR) approach of Heckman, Ichimura and Todd (1997), which models the evolution of the outcome of the comparison group, and the inverse probability weighting (IPW) approach of Abadie (2005), which models the propensity score. Each is consistent only if its own working model is correct, and the two conditions are not nested. The paper combines them into doubly robust (DR) estimands that identify the ATT if either the propensity score model or the outcome regression model for the comparison group is correctly specified, for panel data and for repeated cross-sections.

There are three further contributions. First, the paper derives the semiparametric efficiency bound for the ATT under the DID identifying assumptions for both data structures, shows that panel data allow more efficient estimation than repeated cross-sections, and quantifies the gap. Second, it shows that the DR estimator for panel data is locally efficient, whereas with repeated cross-sections only the DR estimator that also models the outcome of the treated group in both periods attains the bound; the simpler one that mimics the panel formula does not. Third, for a logistic propensity score and linear outcome regressions, it shows that estimating the propensity score by inverse probability tilting and the outcome regression by weighted least squares gives estimators that are also doubly robust for inference: their asymptotic variance has the same form whichever working model is correct. Monte Carlo simulations and an application to the LaLonde job training data illustrate the results. The proofs are in a supplemental appendix; this note reports the statements and the logic the main text gives for them.

Assumptions 2 and 3 are:

E[Y1(0)−Y0(0)∣D=1,X]=E[Y1(0)−Y0(0)∣D=0,X]a.s.P(D=1)>ε,P(D=1∣X)≤1−εa.s. for some ε>0(2)\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)|D=1,X]&=\mathbb{E}[Y_1(0)-Y_0(0)|D=0,X]\quad\text{a.s.}\\ \mathbb{P}(D=1)>\varepsilon,\qquad\mathbb{P}(D=1|X)&\leq1-\varepsilon\quad\text{a.s. for some }\varepsilon>0 \end{aligned} \tag{2}E[Y1​(0)−Y0​(0)∣D=1,X]P(D=1)>ε,P(D=1∣X)​=E[Y1​(0)−Y0​(0)∣D=0,X]a.s.≤1−εa.s. for some ε>0​(2)

The first line is the conditional parallel trends assumption: absent treatment, the average outcomes of treated and comparison units with the same covariates would have evolved in parallel. It allows covariate-specific trends but not unit-specific trends. The second line is overlap: a positive fraction of the population is treated, and at every value of XXX there is some probability of being untreated. No anticipation is built into the notation, since treatment status is zero for everyone at t=0t=0t=0 and the observed pre-treatment outcome is Y0=Y0(0)Y_0=Y_0(0)Y0​=Y0​(0).

Existing Estimands

Theorem 1 (double robustness). Under Assumptions 1 to 3: (a) with panel data, τdr,p=τ\tau^{dr,p}=\tauτdr,p=τ if either π(X)=p(X)\pi(X)=p(X)π(X)=p(X) a.s. or μ0,Δp(X)=m0,1p(X)−m0,0p(X)\mu^p_{0,\Delta}(X)=m^p_{0,1}(X)-m^p_{0,0}(X)μ0,Δp​(X)=m0,1p​(X)−m0,0p​(X) a.s.; (b) with repeated cross-sections, τ1dr,rc=τ2dr,rc=τ\tau^{dr,rc}_1=\tau^{dr,rc}_2=\tauτ1dr,rc​=τ2dr,rc​=τ if either π(X)=p(X)\pi(X)=p(X)π(X)=p(X) a.s. or μ0,Δrc(X)=m0,1rc(X)−m0,0rc(X)\mu^{rc}_{0,\Delta}(X)=m^{rc}_{0,1}(X)-m^{rc}_{0,0}(X)μ0,Δrc​(X)=m0,1rc​(X)−m0,0rc​(X) a.s. Only the model for the change in the comparison group's outcome has to be right, not the models for its levels, and nothing is required of the models for the treated group. The logic is the usual one for DR moments. If the propensity score is right, the weights w0pw^p_0w0p​ make the covariate distribution of the comparison group match that of the treated group, so any function of XXX, including a wrong μ0,Δp\mu^p_{0,\Delta}μ0,Δp​, has the same weighted mean in the two groups and cancels, leaving the IPW estimand. If the outcome model is right, the residual ΔY−μ0,Δp(X)\Delta Y-\mu^p_{0,\Delta}(X)ΔY−μ0,Δp​(X) has conditional mean zero in the comparison group, so the comparison term vanishes for any weights that depend only on XXX, leaving the OR estimand. The two repeated cross-section estimands identify the ATT under the same conditions because, under stationarity, E[g(X)∣D=1]=E[g(X)∣D=1,T=t]\mathbb{E}[g(X)|D=1]=\mathbb{E}[g(X)|D=1,T=t]E[g(X)∣D=1]=E[g(X)∣D=1,T=t] for any integrable ggg and t=0,1t=0,1t=0,1. This applies to μ1,trc(⋅)−μ0,trc(⋅)\mu^{rc}_{1,t}(\cdot)-\mu^{rc}_{0,t}(\cdot)μ1,trc​(⋅)−μ0,trc​(⋅) even when these models are wrong, so the two extra terms in τ2dr,rc\tau^{dr,rc}_2τ2dr,rc​ are zero in the population. Modelling the outcome of the treated group is therefore harmless for identification; its role is efficiency.

Semiparametric Efficiency Bounds

The bounds are nonparametric in the sense that no knowledge of the functional forms of the propensity score or the outcome regressions is assumed, and they incorporate all restrictions implied by Assumptions 1 to 3, including stationarity in the repeated cross-section case. Let md,Δp(x)≡md,1p(x)−md,0p(x)m^p_{d,\Delta}(x)\equiv m^p_{d,1}(x)-m^p_{d,0}(x)md,Δp​(x)≡md,1p​(x)−md,0p​(x) and md,Δrc(X)≡md,1rc(X)−md,0rc(X)m^{rc}_{d,\Delta}(X)\equiv m^{rc}_{d,1}(X)-m^{rc}_{d,0}(X)md,Δrc​(X)≡md,1rc​(X)−md,0rc​(X).

In both cases the first component depends on the conditional ATT, m1,Δ(X)−m0,Δ(X)m_{1,\Delta}(X)-m_{0,\Delta}(X)m1,Δ​(X)−m0,Δ​(X) (the superscripts ppp and rcrcrc are dropped when no confusion arises). The other components differ. With panel data both Y1Y_1Y1​ and Y0Y_0Y0​ are observed for every unit, so the differenced residuals can be reweighted directly. With repeated cross-sections YtY_tYt​ is seen only when T=tT=tT=t, so each of the four cells (D,T)∈{0,1}2(D,T)\in\{0,1\}^2(D,T)∈{0,1}2 has its own weight and its own residual. If stationarity were not imposed in the derivation, the resulting bound would be wider than the one above. The outcome regressions of the treated group also enter asymmetrically, since the panel influence function can be rewritten as:

ηe,p(Y1,Y0,D,X)=(w1p(D)−w0p(D,X;p))(ΔY−m0,Δ(X))−w1p(D)⋅τ(16)\eta^{e,p}(Y_1,Y_0,D,X)=\left(w^p_1(D)-w^p_0(D,X;p)\right)\left(\Delta Y-m_{0,\Delta}(X)\right)-w^p_1(D)\cdot\tau \tag{16}ηe,p(Y1​,Y0​,D,X)=(w1p​(D)−w0p​(D,X;p))(ΔY−m0,Δ​(X))−w1p​(D)⋅τ(16)

which does not involve m1,1(⋅)m_{1,1}(\cdot)m1,1​(⋅) or m1,0(⋅)m_{1,0}(\cdot)m1,0​(⋅), whereas ηe,rc\eta^{e,rc}ηe,rc does. This is why the panel DR estimand needs no outcome model for the treated group to be efficient, while the repeated cross-section estimand does.

Corollary 1 (efficiency loss from repeated cross-sections). Assume in addition that TTT is independent of (Y1,Y0,D,X)(Y_1,Y_0,D,X)(Y1​,Y0​,D,X), which makes the two sampling schemes comparable. Then:

E[ηe,rc(Y,D,T,X)2]−E[ηe,p(Y1,Y0,D,X)2]=1E[D]2E[D(1−λλ(Y1−m1,1(X))+λ1−λ(Y0−m1,0(X)))2+(1−D)p(X)2(1−p(X))2(1−λλ(Y1−m0,1(X))+λ1−λ(Y0−m0,0(X)))2]≥0(17)\begin{aligned} &\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{e,rc}(Y,D,T,X)^2\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\eta^{e,p}(Y_1,Y_0,D,X)^2\right]\\ &=\frac{1}{\mathbb{E}[D]^2}\mathbb{E}\Bigg[D\left(\sqrt{\frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda}}\left(Y_1-m_{1,1}(X)\right)+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}}\left(Y_0-m_{1,0}(X)\right)\right)^2\\ &\quad+\frac{(1-D)p(X)^2}{(1-p(X))^2}\left(\sqrt{\frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda}}\left(Y_1-m_{0,1}(X)\right)+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}}\left(Y_0-m_{0,0}(X)\right)\right)^2\Bigg]\geq0 \end{aligned} \tag{17}​E[ηe,rc(Y,D,T,X)2]−E[ηe,p(Y1​,Y0​,D,X)2]=E[D]21​E[D(λ1−λ​​(Y1​−m1,1​(X))+1−λλ​​(Y0​−m1,0​(X)))2+(1−p(X))2(1−D)p(X)2​(λ1−λ​​(Y1​−m0,1​(X))+1−λλ​​(Y0​−m0,0​(X)))2]≥0​(17)

Panel data therefore allow weakly more efficient estimation. The loss is convex in λ\lambdaλ, so it is larger when the pre-treatment and post-treatment samples are more unbalanced (exactly so when the two variance terms defined next are equal; in general the loss grows as λ\lambdaλ moves away from the optimal value given below). Define, for t=0,1t=0,1t=0,1:

σ~t2=E[D(Yt−m1,t(X))2+(1−D)p(X)2(1−p(X))2(Yt−m0,t(X))2](18)\tilde{\sigma}^2_t=\mathbb{E}\left[D\left(Y_t-m_{1,t}(X)\right)^2+\frac{(1-D)p(X)^2}{(1-p(X))^2}\left(Y_t-m_{0,t}(X)\right)^2\right] \tag{18}σ~t2​=E[D(Yt​−m1,t​(X))2+(1−p(X))2(1−D)p(X)2​(Yt​−m0,t​(X))2](18)

The share of post-treatment observations that minimizes the repeated cross-section bound is λ=σ~1/(σ~0+σ~1)\lambda=\tilde{\sigma}_1/(\tilde{\sigma}_0+\tilde{\sigma}_1)λ=σ~1​/(σ~0​+σ~1​), which equals 0.50.50.5 when σ~02=σ~12\tilde{\sigma}^2_0=\tilde{\sigma}^2_1σ~02​=σ~12​. Since σ~12\tilde{\sigma}^2_1σ~12​ depends on post-treatment outcomes that are unknown at the design stage, the paper regards λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5 as a reasonable default.

Estimators with Generic First Steps

Estimation is in two steps. The nuisance functions are modelled parametrically: π(x;γ)\pi(x;\gamma)π(x;γ) for the propensity score and μd,tp(x;βd,tp)\mu^p_{d,t}(x;\beta^p_{d,t})μd,tp​(x;βd,tp​) or μd,trc(x;βd,trc)\mu^{rc}_{d,t}(x;\beta^{rc}_{d,t})μd,trc​(x;βd,trc​) for the outcome regressions, each known up to a finite-dimensional parameter whose pseudo-true value (γ∗\gamma^*γ∗, βd,t∗,p\beta^{*,p}_{d,t}βd,t∗,p​, βd,t∗,rc\beta^{*,rc}_{d,t}βd,t∗,rc​) is the probability limit of the first-step estimator and is well defined under misspecification. The fitted values are then plugged into the sample analogue of the estimand. For panel data:

τ^dr,p=En[(w^1p(D)−w^0p(D,X;γ^))(ΔY−μ0,Δp(X;β^0,0p,β^0,1p))](19)\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}=\mathbb{E}_n\left[\left(\widehat{w}^p_1(D)-\widehat{w}^p_0(D,X;\widehat{\gamma})\right)\left(\Delta Y-\mu^p_{0,\Delta}\left(X;\widehat{\beta}^p_{0,0},\widehat{\beta}^p_{0,1}\right)\right)\right] \tag{19}τdr,p=En​[(w1p​(D)−w0p​(D,X;γ​))(ΔY−μ0,Δp​(X;β​0,0p​,β​0,1p​))](19)

where w^1p(D)\widehat{w}^p_1(D)w1p​(D) and w^0p(D,X;γ)\widehat{w}^p_0(D,X;\gamma)w0p​(D,X;γ) replace E\mathbb{E}E by En\mathbb{E}_nEn​ and ggg by π(⋅;γ)\pi(\cdot;\gamma)π(⋅;γ) in the population weights, and μ0,Δp(⋅;β0,β1)=μ0,1p(⋅;β1)−μ0,0p(⋅;β0)\mu^p_{0,\Delta}(\cdot;\beta_0,\beta_1)=\mu^p_{0,1}(\cdot;\beta_1)-\mu^p_{0,0}(\cdot;\beta_0)μ0,Δp​(⋅;β0​,β1​)=μ0,1p​(⋅;β1​)−μ0,0p​(⋅;β0​). For repeated cross-sections, τ^1dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_1τ1dr,rc​ is the sample analogue of τ1dr,rc\tau^{dr,rc}_1τ1dr,rc​ with weights w^1rc(D,T)\widehat{w}^{rc}_1(D,T)w1rc​(D,T) and w^0rc(D,T,X;γ^)\widehat{w}^{rc}_0(D,T,X;\widehat{\gamma})w0rc​(D,T,X;γ​), and the second estimator is:

The added terms compare the fitted conditional effect averaged over all treated units with its average over the treated units sampled in period ttt. They vanish in the population but not in the sample, and using all treated observations in both averages is what delivers efficiency.

The asymptotic theory (Appendix A of the paper) requires smooth parametric working models, first-step estimators that are asymptotically linear with influence functions lpsl_{ps}lps​ and lregl_{reg}lreg​, a propensity score model bounded away from one, and weak integrability conditions (Assumptions A.1 and A.2). Further Improved Estimators: Double Robustness for Inference

Suppose the researcher adopts a logistic propensity score and a linear outcome model with the same covariates:

π(X,γ)=Λ(X′γ)≡exp⁡(X′γ)1+exp⁡(X′γ),μ0,Δlin,p(X;β0,Δp)≡X′β0,Δp(25)\pi(X,\gamma)=\Lambda(X'\gamma)\equiv\frac{\exp(X'\gamma)}{1+\exp(X'\gamma)},\qquad\mu^{lin,p}_{0,\Delta}\left(X;\beta^p_{0,\Delta}\right)\equiv X'\beta^p_{0,\Delta} \tag{25}π(X,γ)=Λ(X′γ)≡1+exp(X′γ)exp(X′γ)​,μ0,Δlin,p​(X;β0,Δp​)≡X′β0,Δp​(25)

The improved panel estimator τ^impdr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}_{imp}τimpdr,p​ is the sample analogue of τdr,p\tau^{dr,p}τdr,p with first steps:

γ^ipt=arg⁡max⁡γ∈ΓEn[DX′γ−(1−D)exp⁡(X′γ)]β^0,Δwls,p=arg⁡min⁡b∈ΘEn[Λ(X′γ^ipt)1−Λ(X′γ^ipt)(ΔY−X′b)2∣D=0](26)\begin{aligned} \widehat{\gamma}^{ipt}&=\arg\max_{\gamma\in\Gamma}\mathbb{E}_n\left[DX'\gamma-(1-D)\exp(X'\gamma)\right]\\ \widehat{\beta}^{wls,p}_{0,\Delta}&=\arg\min_{b\in\Theta}\mathbb{E}_n\left[\frac{\Lambda(X'\widehat{\gamma}^{ipt})}{1-\Lambda(X'\widehat{\gamma}^{ipt})}\left(\Delta Y-X'b\right)^2\bigg|D=0\right] \end{aligned} \tag{26}γ​iptβ​0,Δwls,p​​=argγ∈Γmax​En​[DX′γ−(1−D)exp(X′γ)]=argb∈Θmin​En​[1−Λ(X′γ​ipt)Λ(X′γ​ipt)​(ΔY−X′b)2​D=0]​(26)

The first is the inverse probability tilting estimator of Graham, Pinto and Egel (2012), and the second is weighted least squares on the comparison group with the estimated odds as weights. With the logistic and linear working models and a constant in XXX, these conditions reduce to:

E[(DE[D]−exp⁡(X′γ∗)(1−D)E[exp⁡(X′γ∗)(1−D)])X]=0E[exp⁡(X′γ∗)(ΔY−μ0,Δlin,p(X;β0,Δ∗))X∣D=0]=0(28)\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}\left[\left(\frac{D}{\mathbb{E}[D]}-\frac{\exp(X'\gamma^*)(1-D)}{\mathbb{E}[\exp(X'\gamma^*)(1-D)]}\right)X\right]&=0\\ \mathbb{E}\left[\exp(X'\gamma^*)\left(\Delta Y-\mu^{lin,p}_{0,\Delta}\left(X;\beta^*_{0,\Delta}\right)\right)X\Big|D=0\right]&=0 \end{aligned} \tag{28}E[(E[D]D​−E[exp(X′γ∗)(1−D)]exp(X′γ∗)(1−D)​)X]E[exp(X′γ∗)(ΔY−μ0,Δlin,p​(X;β0,Δ∗​))X​D=0]​=0=0​(28)

The first says that the odds-weighted comparison group has the same covariate means as the treated group, which is the first-order condition of the tilting problem. The second says that the odds-weighted residuals of the comparison group are orthogonal to XXX, which is the first-order condition of the weighted least squares problem. Theorem 2. Under Assumptions 1 to 3, A.1 and A.2 and the working models above: (a) if either Λ(X′γ∗,ipt)=p(X)\Lambda(X'\gamma^{*,ipt})=p(X)Λ(X′γ∗,ipt)=p(X) a.s. or X′β0,Δ∗,wls,p=m0,Δp(X)X'\beta^{*,wls,p}_{0,\Delta}=m^p_{0,\Delta}(X)X′β0,Δ∗,wls,p​=m0,Δp​(X) a.s., then τ^impdr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}_{imp}τimpdr,p​ converges in probability to τ\tauτ and n(τ^impdr,p−τimpdr,p)\sqrt{n}(\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}_{imp}-\tau^{dr,p}_{imp})n​(τimpdr,p​−τimpdr,p​) is asymptotically normal with mean zero and variance Vimpp=E[(ηimpdr,p)2]V^p_{imp}=\mathbb{E}[(\eta^{dr,p}_{imp})^2]Vimpp​=E[(ηimpdr,p​)2]; (b) if both hold, ηimpdr,p=ηe,p\eta^{dr,p}_{imp}=\eta^{e,p}ηimpdr,p​=ηe,p a.s. and VimppV^p_{imp}Vimpp​ equals the panel efficiency bound. This generalizes the cross-section result of Vermeulen and Vansteelandt (2015) to DID. The paper warns against using the three no-estimation-effect conditions directly as generic GMM moments, because local identification can fail, in particular when both working models are correct; and a probit propensity score would require numerical integration in the tilting step.

With repeated cross-sections the working models are Λ(X′γ)\Lambda(X'\gamma)Λ(X′γ) and μd,tlin,rc(X;βd,trc)≡X′βd,trc\mu^{lin,rc}_{d,t}(X;\beta^{rc}_{d,t})\equiv X'\beta^{rc}_{d,t}μd,tlin,rc​(X;βd,trc​)≡X′βd,trc​. The improved estimators τ^1,impdr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_{1,imp}τ1,impdr,rc​ and τ^2,impdr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_{2,imp}τ2,impdr,rc​ have the same form as τ^1dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_1τ1dr,rc​ and τ^2dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_2τ2dr,rc​, with γ^ipt\widehat{\gamma}^{ipt}γ​ipt as above and:

β^0,twls,rc=arg⁡min⁡b∈ΘEn[Λ(X′γ^ipt)1−Λ(X′γ^ipt)(Y−X′b)2∣D=0,T=t]β^1,tols,rc=arg⁡min⁡b∈ΘEn[(Y−X′b)2∣D=1,T=t](31)\begin{aligned} \widehat{\beta}^{wls,rc}_{0,t}&=\arg\min_{b\in\Theta}\mathbb{E}_n\left[\frac{\Lambda(X'\widehat{\gamma}^{ipt})}{1-\Lambda(X'\widehat{\gamma}^{ipt})}\left(Y-X'b\right)^2\bigg|D=0,T=t\right]\\ \widehat{\beta}^{ols,rc}_{1,t}&=\arg\min_{b\in\Theta}\mathbb{E}_n\left[\left(Y-X'b\right)^2\Big|D=1,T=t\right] \end{aligned} \tag{31}β​0,twls,rc​β​1,tols,rc​​=argb∈Θmin​En​[1−Λ(X′γ​ipt)Λ(X′γ​ipt)​(Y−X′b)2​D=0,T=t]=argb∈Θmin​En​[(Y−X′b)2​D=1,T=t]​(31)

The treated-group coefficients are estimated by ordinary least squares because their estimation creates no estimation effect, so any method would do. Theorem 3 states that if either Λ(X′γ∗,ipt)=p(X)\Lambda(X'\gamma^{*,ipt})=p(X)Λ(X′γ∗,ipt)=p(X) a.s. or X′β0,1∗,wls,rc−X′β0,0∗,wls,rc=m0,Δrc(X)X'\beta^{*,wls,rc}_{0,1}-X'\beta^{*,wls,rc}_{0,0}=m^{rc}_{0,\Delta}(X)X′β0,1∗,wls,rc​−X′β0,0∗,wls,rc​=m0,Δrc​(X) a.s., both improved estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal with variances Vj,imprcV^{rc}_{j,imp}Vj,imprc​ whose form does not depend on which model is right; if the propensity score and all four outcome models are right, V2,imprcV^{rc}_{2,imp}V2,imprc​ equals the repeated cross-section bound and V1,imprcV^{rc}_{1,imp}V1,imprc​ does not.

Corollary 2 (cost of mimicking the panel formula). When all working models are correct:

V1,imprc−V2,imprc=E[D]−1⋅Var[1−λλ(m1,1rc(X)−m0,1rc(X))+λ1−λ(m1,0rc(X)−m0,0rc(X))∣D=1]≥0(32)V^{rc}_{1,imp}-V^{rc}_{2,imp}=\mathbb{E}[D]^{-1}\cdot Var\left[\sqrt{\frac{1-\lambda}{\lambda}}\left(m^{rc}_{1,1}(X)-m^{rc}_{0,1}(X)\right)+\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{1-\lambda}}\left(m^{rc}_{1,0}(X)-m^{rc}_{0,0}(X)\right)\bigg|D=1\right]\geq0 \tag{32}V1,imprc​−V2,imprc​=E[D]−1⋅Var[λ1−λ​​(m1,1rc​(X)−m0,1rc​(X))+1−λλ​​(m1,0rc​(X)−m0,0rc​(X))​D=1]≥0(32)

The loss is the variance, among the treated, of a weighted sum of the two period-specific gaps between the treated and comparison regressions. It is zero only if this combination does not vary with XXX. The result does not depend on the logistic and linear specifications, and it covers any estimator based on τ1dr,rc\tau^{dr,rc}_1τ1dr,rc​, including that of Zimmert (2019). The paper therefore recommends estimators based on τ2dr,rc\tau^{dr,rc}_2τ2dr,rc​.

Monte Carlo Design and Findings

The designs build on Kang and Schafer (2007). For a generic W=(W1,W2,W3,W4)′W=(W_1,W_2,W_3,W_4)'W=(W1​,W2​,W3​,W4​)′:

freg(W)=210+27.4⋅W1+13.7⋅(W2+W3+W4)fps(W)=0.75⋅(−W1+0.5⋅W2−0.25⋅W3−0.1⋅W4)(33)\begin{aligned} f_{reg}(W)&=210+27.4\cdot W_1+13.7\cdot(W_2+W_3+W_4)\\ f_{ps}(W)&=0.75\cdot(-W_1+0.5\cdot W_2-0.25\cdot W_3-0.1\cdot W_4) \end{aligned} \tag{33}freg​(W)fps​(W)​=210+27.4⋅W1​+13.7⋅(W2​+W3​+W4​)=0.75⋅(−W1​+0.5⋅W2​−0.25⋅W3​−0.1⋅W4​)​(33)

The vector X=(X1,X2,X3,X4)′X=(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)'X=(X1​,X2​,X3​,X4​)′ is standard normal, and Z=(Z1,Z2,Z3,Z4)′Z=(Z_1,Z_2,Z_3,Z_4)'Z=(Z1​,Z2​,Z3​,Z4​)′ consists of standardized nonlinear transformations of XXX (for example the first is based on exp⁡(0.5X1)\exp(0.5X_1)exp(0.5X1​)). Only ZZZ is observed and it enters all working models linearly. In the first design:

Y0(0)=freg(Z)+v(Z,D)+ε0,Y1(d)=2⋅freg(Z)+v(Z,D)+ε1(d),d=0,1p(Z)=exp⁡(fps(Z))1+exp⁡(fps(Z)),D=1{p(Z)≥U}(34)\begin{aligned} Y_0(0)&=f_{reg}(Z)+v(Z,D)+\varepsilon_0,\qquad Y_1(d)=2\cdot f_{reg}(Z)+v(Z,D)+\varepsilon_1(d),\quad d=0,1\\ p(Z)&=\frac{\exp(f_{ps}(Z))}{1+\exp(f_{ps}(Z))},\qquad D=1\{p(Z)\geq U\} \end{aligned} \tag{34}Y0​(0)p(Z)​=freg​(Z)+v(Z,D)+ε0​,Y1​(d)=2⋅freg​(Z)+v(Z,D)+ε1​(d),d=0,1=1+exp(fps​(Z))exp(fps​(Z))​,D=1{p(Z)≥U}​(34)

where ε0\varepsilon_0ε0​ and ε1(d)\varepsilon_1(d)ε1​(d) are independent standard normal, UUU is standard uniform, and v(W,D)v(W,D)v(W,D) is normal with mean D⋅freg(W)D\cdot f_{reg}(W)D⋅freg​(W) and variance one, playing the role of time-invariant unobserved heterogeneity. The true ATT is zero, and there are covariate-specific trends. DGP1 has both working models correct. DGP2 replaces ZZZ by XXX in the propensity score (OR correct, propensity score wrong), DGP3 replaces ZZZ by XXX in the outcome equations (propensity score correct, OR wrong), and DGP4 does both. The sample size is n=1000n=1000n=1000 with 10,000 replications; for repeated cross-sections each unit is observed in one period only, with T=1{UT≤λ}T=1\{U_T\leq\lambda\}T=1{UT​≤λ} and λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5. Besides the estimators above, the comparison includes the Hajek type IPW estimators with normalized weights, τ^stdipw,p\widehat{\tau}^{ipw,p}_{std}τstdipw,p​ and τ^stdipw,rc\widehat{\tau}^{ipw,rc}_{std}τstdipw,rc​, obtained by setting the outcome models to zero in τ^dr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}τdr,p and τ^1dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_1τ1dr,rc​.

  • TWFE: the average bias of τ^fe\widehat{\tau}^{fe}τfe is between −13.2-13.2−13.2 and −21.0-21.0−21.0 in all four panel designs, with coverage of 95 percent confidence intervals essentially zero, because the specification rules out covariate-specific trends.

  • Panel, both models correct (bound 11.1): all semiparametric estimators are nearly unbiased. The average estimated asymptotic variance is 11.1 for τ^dr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}τdr,p and 10.9 for τ^impdr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}_{imp}τimpdr,p​, against 10.2 for τ^reg\widehat{\tau}^{reg}τreg (which uses more assumptions), 8078.0 for τ^ipw,p\widehat{\tau}^{ipw,p}τipw,p and 1286.4 for τ^stdipw,p\widehat{\tau}^{ipw,p}_{std}τstdipw,p​. The root mean square errors are 0.106, 0.106, 0.100, 2.774 and 1.132. Normalizing the IPW weights matters a great deal.

  • Panel, one model wrong: with only the OR correct, the DR estimators match τ^reg\widehat{\tau}^{reg}τreg (bias −0.001-0.001−0.001), while the IPW estimators are biased (2.010 and −0.794-0.794−0.794, coverage 0.838 and 0.856). With only the propensity score correct, τ^reg\widehat{\tau}^{reg}τreg is biased (−1.384-1.384−1.384, coverage 0.800), while the DR and IPW estimators are not; the root mean square error is 1.214 for τ^dr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}τdr,p and 1.015 for τ^impdr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}_{imp}τimpdr,p​, against 3.198 and 1.427 for the two IPW estimators. In this design the variances are far above the bound (1400.9 and 971.2).

  • Panel, both wrong: every estimator is biased. The DR estimators (−3.188-3.188−3.188 and −2.529-2.529−2.529) do better than τ^reg\widehat{\tau}^{reg}τreg (−5.204-5.204−5.204) and normalized IPW (−3.954-3.954−3.954), but the Horvitz-Thompson IPW estimator has the smallest bias (−1.085-1.085−1.085).

  • Repeated cross-sections: the bound is 44.4 with a correct propensity score (46.4 otherwise), four times the panel value. With both models correct, the estimated variance is 44.4 for τ^2dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_2τ2dr,rc​ and 42.1 for τ^2,impdr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_{2,imp}τ2,impdr,rc​, but 9222.0 for τ^1dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_1τ1dr,rc​ and 9220.1 for τ^1,impdr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_{1,imp}τ1,impdr,rc​; the root mean square errors are 0.216 against 3.041, compared with 7.588 for OR, 9.648 for normalized IPW and 55.971 for Horvitz-Thompson IPW. The loss in Corollary 2 is thus of first order. With the OR wrong and the propensity score correct, the improved estimators help: the root mean square error is 5.692, 4.742, 4.837 and 4.062 for τ^1dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_1τ1dr,rc​, τ^2dr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_2τ2dr,rc​, τ^1,impdr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_{1,imp}τ1,impdr,rc​ and τ^2,impdr,rc\widehat{\tau}^{dr,rc}_{2,imp}τ2,impdr,rc​.

Empirical Application: NSW Job Training

The application revisits LaLonde (1986), following Smith and Todd (2005). Three experimental samples of the National Supported Work (NSW) program are used: the original LaLonde sample, the Dehejia-Wahba (DW) sample, and the early random assignment (early RA) subsample of the DW sample, each combined with a non-experimental comparison group from the Current Population Survey (CPS). The outcome is real earnings in 1978, the pre-treatment outcome Y0Y_0Y0​ is real earnings in 1975, and the covariates are age, years of education, real earnings in 1974 and dummies for high school dropout, married, black and Hispanic. The experimental benchmarks for the ATT are 886 dollars (standard error 488), 1794 dollars (671) and 2748 dollars (1005). The exercise estimates the evaluation bias: each DID estimator is applied to the randomized-out experimental controls as a pseudo-treated group and the CPS sample as comparison group. Since the controls received no training, the true effect is zero and any deviation is bias. Three covariate specifications are used: linear; DW (adding a dummy for zero earnings in 1974, age squared, age cubed divided by 1000, schooling squared and schooling times 1974 earnings); and augmented DW (adding interactions of married with 1974 earnings and with zero 1974 earnings).

  • TWFE: the estimated bias is 868 dollars in the LaLonde sample, 2092 in the DW sample and 1136 in the early RA sample under every specification, that is 98, 117 and 41 percent of the benchmarks; it is stable, large, positive and mostly statistically significant.

  • OR: τ^reg\widehat{\tau}^{reg}τreg has the smallest standard errors (350 to 360 in the LaLonde sample) but is severely biased downward there: −1301-1301−1301, −830-830−830 and −1041-1041−1041 dollars under the three specifications.

  • IPW: τ^ipw,p\widehat{\tau}^{ipw,p}τipw,p has the largest standard errors (for example 845 in the DW sample with the DW specification, against 672 with normalized weights) and relatively small biases.

  • DR: in the DW sample the bias of τ^dr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}τdr,p is 253 (standard error 451), 408 (691) and 514 (663) dollars, and that of τ^impdr,p\widehat{\tau}^{dr,p}_{imp}τimpdr,p​ is 253 (452), 520 (588) and 524 (582). In the early RA sample the biases are −434-434−434 (605), −246-246−246 (724) and −148-148−148 (701) against −441-441−441 (607), −176-176−176 (683) and −144-144−144 (677), that is 5 to 16 percent of the benchmark in absolute value. In the LaLonde sample they are −871-871−871 (396), −626-626−626 (496) and −597-597−597 (491) against −901-901−901 (394), −591-591−591 (467) and −599-599−599 (470). The DR estimators share the small biases of IPW with smaller standard errors, and the improved version is more precise under the two richer specifications.

References

  • Sant'Anna, Pedro HC and Jun Zhao. 2020. “Doubly Robust Difference-in-Differences Estimators.” Journal of Econometrics, 219(1): 101–122.

This defines the target parameter, the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT). Y1(1)Y_1(1)Y1​(1) and Y1(0)Y_1(0)Y1​(0) are the post-treatment potential outcomes with and without treatment, and the expectation is taken over the treated subpopulation D=1D=1D=1 only, so τ\tauτ is measured in the units of the outcome and answers the question of how much the treatment changed the period-1 outcome of those who actually received it. Nothing is said about the effect on the untreated, which is why the overlap condition in equation (2) is one-sided.

The second equality uses the observation rule Y1=DY1(1)+(1−D)Y1(0)Y_1=DY_1(1)+(1-D)Y_1(0)Y1​=DY1​(1)+(1−D)Y1​(0): for a treated unit the observed outcome is Y1(1)Y_1(1)Y1​(1), so the first term is a population moment of observed data,

E[Y1(1)∣D=1]=E[Y1∣D=1].\mathbb{E}[Y_1(1)|D=1]=\mathbb{E}[Y_1|D=1].E[Y1​(1)∣D=1]=E[Y1​∣D=1].

The second term, E[Y1(0)∣D=1]\mathbb{E}[Y_1(0)|D=1]E[Y1​(0)∣D=1], is the mean outcome the treated would have had without treatment. It is never observed, and the whole identification problem is to express it through observables. Equation (2) gives the assumptions that do so, and every estimand in the note (equations (3), (4), (7), (9) and (10)) is a different way of writing this counterfactual mean. The effect is allowed to be heterogeneous across units and across values of XXX; τ\tauτ averages the conditional effect E[Y1(1)−Y1(0)∣D=1,X]\mathbb{E}[Y_1(1)-Y_1(0)|D=1,X]E[Y1​(1)−Y1​(0)∣D=1,X] over the covariate distribution of the treated.

The first line is the conditional parallel trends assumption (Assumption 2). These are the two working models under which the improved estimator is built. The propensity score is logistic: Λ\LambdaΛ maps the index X′γX'\gammaX′γ into (0,1)(0,1)(0,1), and each element of γ\gammaγ is the effect of a covariate on the log odds of treatment. The model for the change in the comparison group's outcome is linear in the same covariates, X′β0,ΔpX'\beta^p_{0,\Delta}X′β0,Δp​; the paper notes that μ0,Δp(X;β0,0p,β0,1p)\mu^p_{0,\Delta}(X;\beta^p_{0,0},\beta^p_{0,1})μ0,Δp​(X;β0,0p​,β0,1p​) is modelled directly as one linear function, so β0,Δp\beta^p_{0,\Delta}β0,Δp​ plays the role of β0,1p−β0,0p\beta^p_{0,1}-\beta^p_{0,0}β0,1p​−β0,0p​. Since the first element of XXX is a constant, both models have intercepts, and XXX may contain transformations and interactions, so linear means linear in parameters.

The logistic form is chosen because of two algebraic facts used in equations (26) to (28):

Since W1W_1W1​ raises the outcome index and lowers the treatment probability, the treated have systematically lower values of fregf_{reg}freg​: selection into treatment is correlated with the determinants of the outcome, and because the index is multiplied by two in the post-treatment period (equation (34)), also with the outcome trend. Unconditional parallel trends therefore fails and covariate adjustment is essential. Both indices are linear, so a linear outcome regression and a logistic propensity score in the argument that is actually used to generate the data are correctly specified; misspecification is created by generating the data with XXX while the researcher only observes the nonlinear transformations ZZZ.

This is the first data-generating process (DGP1), in which both working models are correct because the observed ZZZ enters outcomes and treatment through the linear indices of equation (33). The pre-treatment untreated outcome is the index plus a time-invariant heterogeneity term v(Z,D)v(Z,D)v(Z,D), normal with mean D⋅freg(Z)D\cdot f_{reg}(Z)D⋅freg​(Z) and unit variance, plus a standard normal shock. In the post-treatment period the index is doubled, the same vvv enters, and the shocks ε1(1)\varepsilon_1(1)ε1​(1) and ε1(0)\varepsilon_1(0)ε1​(0) both have mean zero.
